--- title: "Choosing a method" description: "The most flexible method is often not the right one. A few questions about the aim, the data and the audience narrow the choice, and on the survey's new sites a curve built for counts predicts as well as any of the section's flexible methods." order: 7 categories: [supervised, regression, trees-ensembles] --- ## The question comes before the method The section's methods range from a straight line to hundreds of trees. None of them is best everywhere, and the most flexible one is often not the right one. A few questions about the aim, the data and the people who will use the result narrow the choice before any model is fitted. This page sets out those questions and then scores the section's methods for counts on the same new sites. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Five questions narrow the choice [Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) separated the two aims: explaining needs a model whose parts can be read, while predicting can use anything that works on new data. The kind of outcome comes next. A quantity suits [linear regression](linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd), a count [Poisson regression](count-regression.qmd) and a yes-or-no answer [logistic regression](logistic-regression.qmd). k-nearest neighbours, trees, forests and boosting handle any kind of outcome, but they assume no shape, so they must learn it from the data. The other three questions depend on how the model will be used. Beyond its data, a regression model follows its fitted shape, which may or may not be true, while the neighbours and the tree models stay level; [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) deals with predicting outside the data. Flexible models need many examples to learn their shape; with a few hundred noisy ones, a curve with a few terms often does as well. And a model that has to convince a manager or a reviewer must be one they can check. ::: {.diagram} ![Five questions narrow the choice of method: the aim, the kind of outcome, whether predictions are needed beyond the sampled range, how much data there is, and who has to accept the result.](img/choosing-a-method.svg){fig-alt="Five cards, one question each. The aim, predict or explain: to explain, choose a model whose parts can be read, regression coefficients or a short tree. The outcome, quantity, count or yes/no: quantity, linear or polynomial regression; count, Poisson or negative binomial; yes/no, logistic. The range, beyond the sampled range: neighbours and tree models stay level past the data; a regression model follows its shape, right or wrong. The data, hundreds or thousands: a few hundred noisy examples suit a simple curve; many thousands give the flexible methods room. The audience, who must accept it: people can check a short tree or a regression model; hundreds of trees need extra tools to explain. A note says: when unsure, fit a regression model and a forest; if the forest wins by a lot, the regression model is missing a shape."} ::: ## Worked example The outcome is the count of the species at each station. The data, the split by site and the fitting and validation sites are those of the last four pages. Seven models are compared: linear and polynomial regression, Poisson regression, k-nearest neighbours, the decision tree, the random forest and boosting. The number of neighbours, the tree's depth and the boosted model's number of trees are chosen on the validation sites, as on the pages that introduced them. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) fit_split <- group_initial_split(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) fitting <- training(fit_split) validation <- testing(fit_split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season line_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) curve_recipe <- line_recipe |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) knn_recipe <- line_recipe |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) tree_recipe <- line_recipe boost_recipe <- line_recipe |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) knn_model <- function(k) { nearest_neighbor(neighbors = k, weight_func = "rectangular") |> set_mode("regression") } tree_model <- function(depth) { decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = depth, min_n = 2, cost_complexity = 0) } boost_model <- function(trees) { boost_tree(mode = "regression", trees = trees, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.05) } validation_rmse <- function(workflow) { fitted <- fit(workflow, fitting) rmse_vec(validation$abundance, predict(fitted, validation)$.pred) } best_of <- function(values, make) { scores <- map_dbl(values, \(v) validation_rmse(make(v))) values[which.min(scores)] } ks <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100, 150, 200, 300) best_k <- best_of(ks, \(k) workflow(knn_recipe, knn_model(k))) best_depth <- best_of(1:15, \(d) workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(d))) best_boost <- best_of(c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600), \(n) workflow(boost_recipe, boost_model(n))) models <- list( "Linear regression" = workflow(line_recipe, linear_reg()), "Polynomial regression" = workflow(curve_recipe, linear_reg()), "Poisson regression" = workflow(curve_recipe, poisson_reg()), "k-nearest neighbours" = workflow(knn_recipe, knn_model(best_k)), "Decision tree" = workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(best_depth)), "Random forest" = workflow(tree_recipe, rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 400) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123)), "Boosting" = workflow(boost_recipe, boost_model(best_boost)) ) c(k = best_k, depth = best_depth, trees = best_boost) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> k depth trees #> 30 5 200 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.base import clone from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, PoissonRegressor from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] inner = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) fit_rows, val_rows = next(inner.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) fitting, validation = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[val_rows] dummies = OneHotEncoder(drop=["gravel", "spring"], sparse_output=False) line_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", dummies, categorical), ]) def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", dummies, categorical), ]) knn_recipe = Pipeline([("columns", line_recipe), ("standardise", StandardScaler())]) tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) def pipeline(recipe, model): return Pipeline([("recipe", clone(recipe)), ("model", model)]) def validation_rmse(workflow): fitted = workflow.fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]) return root_mean_squared_error(validation["abundance"], fitted.predict(validation[predictors])) def best_of(values, make): scores = [validation_rmse(make(v)) for v in values] return values[int(np.argmin(scores))] def boost_model(trees): return GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=trees, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=123) best_k = best_of([1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100, 150, 200, 300], lambda k: pipeline(knn_recipe, KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k))) best_depth = best_of(list(range(1, 16)), lambda d: pipeline( tree_recipe, DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d, random_state=123))) best_boost = best_of([1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600], lambda n: pipeline(tree_recipe, boost_model(n))) models = { "Linear regression": pipeline(line_recipe, LinearRegression()), "Polynomial regression": pipeline(curve_recipe, LinearRegression()), "Poisson regression": pipeline(curve_recipe, PoissonRegressor( alpha=0, solver="newton-cholesky")), "k-nearest neighbours": pipeline(knn_recipe, KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=best_k)), "Decision tree": pipeline(tree_recipe, DecisionTreeRegressor( max_depth=best_depth, random_state=123)), "Random forest": pipeline(tree_recipe, RandomForestRegressor( n_estimators=400, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123)), "Boosting": pipeline(tree_recipe, boost_model(best_boost)), } {"k": best_k, "depth": best_depth, "trees": best_boost} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> {'k': 50, 'depth': 5, 'trees': 25} ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Validation and test sites rank the models differently Each model is fitted twice: on the fitting sites and scored on the validation sites, and on all the training sites and scored once on the test sites, with the [RMSE](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#the-test-error-is-a-typical-miss) and [$R^2$](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd#one-linear-regression-shows-each-kind). The last column counts the test stations predicted to hold fewer than zero animals. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions <- map(models, \(w) list( validation = predict(fit(w, fitting), validation)$.pred, test = predict(fit(w, train), test)$.pred )) results <- imap(predictions, \(p, model) tibble( model = model, validation_rmse = rmse_vec(validation$abundance, p$validation), test_rmse = rmse_vec(test$abundance, p$test), test_rsq = rsq_trad_vec(test$abundance, p$test), below_zero = sum(p$test < 0) )) |> list_rbind() |> arrange(test_rmse) results |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | validation_rmse| test_rmse| test_rsq| below_zero| |:---------------------|---------------:|---------:|--------:|----------:| |Poisson regression | 3.68| 3.55| 0.23| 0| |Polynomial regression | 3.76| 3.62| 0.19| 12| |Linear regression | 3.95| 3.75| 0.14| 1| |k-nearest neighbours | 3.91| 3.83| 0.10| 0| |Random forest | 3.77| 3.96| 0.04| 0| |Boosting | 3.79| 4.35| -0.16| 0| |Decision tree | 3.63| 4.48| -0.23| 0|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def predict(workflow, data, new_data): fitted = workflow.fit(data[predictors], data["abundance"]) return fitted.predict(new_data[predictors]) predictions = {name: {"validation": predict(w, fitting, validation), "test": predict(w, train, test)} for name, w in models.items()} results = pd.DataFrame([{ "model": name, "validation_rmse": root_mean_squared_error(validation["abundance"], p["validation"]), "test_rmse": root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], p["test"]), "test_rsq": r2_score(test["abundance"], p["test"]), "below_zero": int((p["test"] < 0).sum()), } for name, p in predictions.items()]).sort_values("test_rmse") results.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | model | validation_rmse | test_rmse | test_rsq | below_zero | |---:|:----------------------|------------------:|------------:|-----------:|-------------:| | 1 | Polynomial regression | 4.55 | 4.73 | 0.26 | 10 | | 5 | Random forest | 4.58 | 4.77 | 0.25 | 0 | | 2 | Poisson regression | 4.63 | 4.82 | 0.23 | 0 | | 0 | Linear regression | 4.65 | 4.9 | 0.21 | 1 | | 6 | Boosting | 4.6 | 4.99 | 0.18 | 0 | | 3 | k-nearest neighbours | 4.61 | 5.05 | 0.16 | 0 | | 4 | Decision tree | 4.7 | 5.7 | -0.07 | 0 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} results |> mutate(model = fct_rev(fct_inorder(model))) |> pivot_longer(c(validation_rmse, test_rmse), names_to = "sites", values_to = "rmse") |> mutate(sites = if_else(sites == "test_rmse", "test", "validation")) |> ggplot(aes(rmse, model)) + geom_line(aes(group = model), colour = "#c9d1d7", linewidth = 1.6) + geom_point(aes(colour = sites), size = 3.4) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(validation = ml_palette[["orange"]], test = ml_palette[["blue"]]), breaks = c("validation", "test"), labels = c("Validation sites", "Test sites")) + labs(x = "RMSE (individuals)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "Two sets of new sites rank the models differently") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The RMSE of each model on the validation sites (fitted on the fitting sites) and on the test sites (fitted on all the training sites), ordered by the test score. The number of neighbours, the tree's depth and the boosted model's number of trees were chosen on the validation sites.](choosing-a-method_files/figure-html/fig-comparison-1.png){#fig-comparison fig-alt='Dot chart of RMSE for seven models, one row each, with a validation point and a test point joined by a line. Poisson regression is at the top with the lowest test error, followed by polynomial and linear regression and k-nearest neighbours. The random forest, boosting and the decision tree come last on the test sites, although the tree has the lowest validation error of all seven.' width=1600} ::: ::: ::: On the 40 test sites, Poisson regression comes first, with an RMSE of 3.55 and an $R^2$ of 0.23. Polynomial regression is close behind at 3.62, but it predicted fewer than zero animals at 12 test stations, which Poisson regression cannot do. Linear regression and k-nearest neighbours follow, and the three tree models come last; the single tree and boosting have an $R^2$ below zero. The validation sites tell a different story. There the tree scores best of all, at 3.63. Part of that is because its depth was chosen to suit those same sites, so its validation score flatters it; the test sites were kept apart for exactly this reason. The rest is chance: 27 validation sites and 40 test sites are small samples, and close models can swap places on the next set. The Python tab, with its own split, puts polynomial regression and the forest ahead of Poisson regression. [Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) shows how far such differences can be trusted. What the survey does show is the pattern in the diagram: 598 noisy training stations are too few for the flexible methods to learn a shape that a curve with a few terms already describes, and matching the model to the kind of outcome, counts here, helped at least as much as flexibility. ### Beyond the sampled temperatures each model follows its own rule The training stations span 1.9 to 16 °C. @fig-extrapolate asks three of the models for predictions from 0 to 22 °C, with the other inputs held at typical values. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} temp_range <- range(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE) grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(0, 22, length.out = 300), depth_m = median(train$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3, na.rm = TRUE), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu, na.rm = TRUE), substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)), season = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season)) ) shown <- c("Linear regression", "Poisson regression", "Random forest") curves <- map(shown, \(m) augment(fit(models[[m]], train), grid) |> mutate(model = m)) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(model = factor(model, levels = shown)) ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, .pred, colour = model)) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = temp_range[1], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.12) + annotate("rect", xmin = temp_range[2], xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.12) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Linear regression" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Poisson regression" = ml_palette[["green"]], "Random forest" = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count", colour = NULL, title = "Beyond the data each model follows its own rule") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Predicted count across temperature from linear regression, Poisson regression and the random forest, all fitted on the training sites, with the other inputs held at typical values (sand, summer, median depth, chlorophyll and salinity). The shaded ends lie beyond the temperatures of the training stations.](choosing-a-method_files/figure-html/fig-extrapolate-1.png){#fig-extrapolate fig-alt='Three lines of predicted count against temperature from 0 to 22 degrees. The Poisson regression curve is a smooth hump peaking near 8 degrees; the forest is a jagged line with its highest values in the same middle region; the linear regression line falls steadily from left to right. In the shaded regions beyond the training temperatures the forest stays level at either end, the Poisson regression curve flattens towards zero, and the linear regression line keeps falling until it predicts fewer than zero animals near 20 degrees.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: Inside the sampled range Poisson regression and the forest share a peak in the middle temperatures, and the linear regression line cuts across it. Beyond the range, each does what its form dictates. The forest stays level at about 1.7, because no tree has a question about warmer water. Poisson regression flattens towards zero, from 0.1 at the edge of the data to almost nothing at 22 °C. Linear regression keeps falling at its fitted rate and predicts fewer than zero animals from 18.8 °C. Nothing in the data says which of the first two is right. A forecast for warmer water rests on the assumption built into the model, so choose a model whose assumption you can defend, and say what it is. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Choose a method from the aim, the kind of outcome, whether predictions are needed beyond the sampled range, the amount of data and who must accept the result, not from which method is most flexible. - On the survey's test sites Poisson regression predicted best and the tree models came last: 598 noisy stations are too few for the flexible methods to beat a curve with a few terms. - Polynomial regression came close, but predicted fewer than zero animals at 12 test stations. A model that matches the outcome cannot make that mistake. - The validation and test sites ranked the models differently. One split cannot separate models that are close, and a model tuned on the validation sites looks best there. - Beyond the data the neighbours and the tree models stay level and a regression model follows its fitted shape; the data check neither. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Change `set.seed(123)` to `set.seed(456)` and re-run the page. Which models change places on the test sites, and does Poisson regression still come first? 2. Give the random forest `curve_recipe` in place of `tree_recipe`, so it also sees the squared depth and temperature. Does its test RMSE change? A tree can already cut an input at any value, so think about what a squared column adds.
